newsitem.title: FRANCE: GAN sale risks another privatisation row in France.
newsitem.headline: GAN sale risks another privatisation row in France.

text.p: Warnings by French insurer GAN that it will need new state money before being privatised could be a play to ensure its future and prevent the sale of its money-spinning CIC banking unit, insurance analysts say.
Chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud "is making the situation look as catastrophic as possible," said a Paris analyst.
Analysts say that unless the government changes course, GAN could go the way of state-owned electronics group Thomson, which is being sold for a symbolic one franc (19 cents).
"I don't see the state floating GAN (Groupe des Assurances Nationales) on the stockmarket. I see it more being given to another company for a franc," said a second analyst.

The planned sale of Thomson, saddled with huge debts, to Lagardere and Daewoo Electronics of Korea has sparked outrage among the French. Opposition leaders and unions are incensed at Lagardere's plan to sell the Thomson Multimedia (TMM) unit to a foreign group for small change after a costly 11 billion franc state recapitalisation.
Bonnaud, announcing a 1.8 billion franc half year loss by 80-percent state-owned GAN last week, said the group, France's third largest insurer, would also have to be recapitalised.

The warning comes at a bad time for the government, battling to reduce spending and cut its deficit to qualify for European monetary union. Bonnaud said GAN hoped to be sold next year despite its expectation of another big loss for 1996.

He would not say how much GAN would need to maintain its solvency ratios following the planned sale of 67 percent of its CIC bank and clean-up of the group's property troubles but analysts say it could be eight billion francs or more. That would be on top of 2.8 billion francs it has already received.
The government has until year end to select a bid for CIC, whose sale has been billed as a prelude to GAN's privatisation.

But there has been strong political opposition to the CIC sale intended to generate cash for GAN. There has also been a shortage of bids because of the government's insistence that the buyer preserve CIC's bancassurance links with GAN along with its regional banking network and maintain jobs.
There has been speculation the government may pull the sale, but so far it insists it is going ahead.
BNP and Societe Generale, the two suitors in the running for CIC, are said to be offering far less for the bank than its 14.6 billion franc book value.

Analysts say GAN would need around 4.5 billion francs to compensate for the expected loss on the CIC sale. And the group, which has been hammered by France's long-running real estate slump, would need another three to four billion francs to compensate for losses on property sales.
Bonnaud has long been unhappy about the government's demand that GAN sell CIC, which distributes a big portion of its insurance premiums and is a money earner for the group.
But even if the government recapitalised GAN by eight billion francs, it would only restore its shareholders' equity to its current 12 billion francs -- enough for a state company.

Analysts say that to survive as a private company, its equity would have to be far larger and GAN would need a buyer with deep pockets. "The average equity of companies with the same turnover is around 18 to 19 billion francs," a Paris analyst said.
"GAN could be sold for a nominal sum and the purchaser would pay for it by putting in the money it needs," said an analyst.

Some analysts say if Bonnaud had his way, GAN would keep CIC, and the insurer would be recapitalised through a capital increase subscribed to by two or three foreign buyers who would initially take a total 40 percent stake in the enlarged group.
Under that scenario, the state would gradually sell off its stake to them over a two- or three-year period. Analysts cite Dutch financial group Fortis as a possible partner.
Analysts say money-losing GAN would have to be sold through a private placement as a flotation was out of the question.

GAN's shares have slid from a year high of 188.90 francs to 120 on Wednesday, and with France's largest insurer UAP trading way below its privatisation price, retail investors would be leery of putting any money into GAN.
($ = 5.110 French Francs)
